chunks: Automated optical inspection (AOI). The question: What is automated optical inspection (AOI)? What can it capture?
Automated optical inspection (AOI) is a machine with cameras and controlled lights that scans a finished board and looks for visible defects.
It checks that parts are present, in the right place and the right way round, and that the solder looks right.
It is fast and needs no probes, but it can only judge what it can see.
Think of the spot-the-difference puzzle, done at high speed.
The machine knows what a good board looks like, then looks at yours under lights from several angles and flags anything that differs.
Shadows and glints from the different lights help it judge the shape of each solder joint.
The limit is just like the puzzle: it sees only the surface, so anything hidden under a part is invisible to it.
Side view of one chip part with its solder fillets (grey wedges at each end).
Light from low angles reflects off the sloped fillets: a proper concave fillet returns a characteristic bright band to the camera, a missing or poor joint does not.
That is why lighting angle and colour are programmed per defect type.
Reference: what the machine compares against, either a known-good board or rules from the design data. Solder bridge: unwanted solder joining two neighboring pins.
Tombstone: a small chip part standing on one end, joined at only one side. False call: a good feature wrongly flagged as bad. Escape: a real defect that the machine misses.
Say the camera sensor is 4,000 pixels wide and each pixel covers 15 µm. It sees a strip 4,000 x 15 µm = 60 mm wide. A tiny 0201 part is 0.
6 mm long, so it spans 40 pixels, plenty to judge its position. Now count errors. If a board has 1,000 checked features and 0.
1 % of good ones are falsely flagged, that is one false alarm per board, which would swamp the human reviewer. That is the whole idea.
"AOI is camera-based inspection of an assembled board, usually after reflow.

Multi-angle lighting and cameras image each component and joint, and software compares them to a golden board or CAD rules to flag missing, shifted, rotated or tombstoned parts, bridges and bad fillets.
It's fast and needs no fixture, but it only sees the surface: no hidden BGA joints, no component values, no function, so it's combined with X-ray, ICT and functional test."
